title: A2 Writing Quiz 1 — Doctor Visits & Everyday Habits

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never see snow in Baku.
I have never seen snow in Baku.
I never have seen snow in Baku.
I have never saw snow in Baku.
questions.explanation: Present perfect: have/has + past participle: 'I have never seen snow in Baku.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She has visited the doctor yesterday.
She visited the doctor yesterday.
She has visit the doctor yesterday.
She visits the doctor yesterday ago.
questions.explanation: A specific past time ('yesterday') needs past simple, not present perfect.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: It was raining when I left home.
It rained when I was leaving home.
It was rain when I left home.
It raining was when I left home.
questions.explanation: Past continuous (background action) + past simple (interrupting action): 'It was raining when I left home.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Today is more colder than yesterday.
Today is colder than yesterday.
Today is coldest than yesterday.
Today is more cold as yesterday.
questions.explanation: Short adjectives take -er for comparatives: 'colder than'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This is the worst headache I've ever had.
This is the more worst headache I've ever had.
This is worse headache I've ever had.
This is the most worst headache I've ever had.
questions.explanation: Irregular superlative of 'bad' is 'the worst': 'the worst headache'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: You should to see a doctor.
You should seeing a doctor.
You should see a doctor.
You should sees a doctor.
questions.explanation: 'Should' is followed by the base form of the verb: 'should see'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He have to take this medicine twice a day.
He has to take this medicine twice a day.
He has to taking this medicine twice a day.
He has to took this medicine twice a day.
questions.explanation: Third person singular: 'has to' + base verb: 'has to take'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: You mustn't to eat before the test.
You mustn't eat before the test.
You not must eat before the test.
You don't must eat before the test.
questions.explanation: 'Mustn't' + base verb expresses prohibition: 'mustn't eat'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Look at those clouds! It's going to rain.
Look at those clouds! It will to rain.
Look at those clouds! It's going rain.
Look at those clouds! It going to rains.
questions.explanation: 'Going to' + base verb is used for predictions based on present evidence: 'It's going to rain.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If it rains, we will stay at home.
If it will rain, we stay at home.
If it rains, we stayed at home.
If it will rains, we will stay at home.
questions.explanation: First conditional: If + present simple, will + base verb: 'If it rains, we will stay at home.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I enjoy to play tennis on weekends.
I enjoy playing tennis on weekends.
I enjoy play tennis on weekends.
I enjoy played tennis on weekends.
questions.explanation: 'Enjoy' is followed by a gerund (-ing form): 'enjoy playing'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm happy hearing you feel better.
I'm happy to hear you feel better.
I'm happy hear you feel better.
I'm happy for hear you feel better.
questions.explanation: Adjective + infinitive: 'happy to hear'.

questions.question: There isn't ___ snow this winter.
options: many
much
a few
several
questions.explanation: 'Snow' is uncountable, so use 'much' in negative sentences.

questions.question: I have ___ free time this week because I'm busy with exams.
options: few
a few
little
many
questions.explanation: 'Time' is uncountable, and 'little' means 'not much'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses 'although'.
options: Although it was cold, we went for a walk.
Although it was cold, but we went for a walk.
It was cold, although we went for a walk but.
Although we went, it was cold for a walk.
questions.explanation: 'Although' introduces a contrast clause and doesn't need 'but': 'Although it was cold, we went for a walk.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The match was cancelled because of the heavy rain.
The match was cancelled because the heavy rain.
The match was cancelled because of heavy raining.
The match was cancelled because heavy of the rain.
questions.explanation: 'Because of' is followed by a noun phrase: 'because of the heavy rain.'

questions.question: I have had this cough ___ three days.
options: since
for
during
from
questions.explanation: 'For' is used with a period of time: 'for three days.'

questions.question: She has felt tired ___ Monday.
options: for
since
during
at
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a starting point in time: 'since Monday.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I feel sick.")
options: She said that she feels sick.
She said that she felt sick.
She said that she is feeling sick.
She said she feel sick.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present simple usually shifts to past simple: 'she felt sick.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a doctor's clinic asking about opening hours?
options: Hey there,
Dear Sir/Madam,
Hiya,
What's up,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir/Madam,' is used when writing formally to an organization without a known name.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a clinic you don't personally know?
options: See you soon,
Yours faithfully,
Bye for now,
Take care,
questions.explanation: 'Yours faithfully,' is used when the recipient's name is unknown, matching 'Dear Sir/Madam,'.

questions.question: Choose the correct suggestion.
options: Why don't we go for a walk if it stops raining?
Why we don't go for a walk if it stops raining?
Why not we go for a walk if it stops raining?
Why don't we going for a walk if it stops raining?
questions.explanation: 'Why don't we' + base verb is a common way to make a suggestion: 'Why don't we go...'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the medicine.' and 'The medicine helped me feel better.'?
options: This is the medicine who helped me feel better.
This is the medicine which helped me feel better.
This is the medicine what helped me feel better.
This is the medicine helped me feel better which.
questions.explanation: 'Which' is used for things in relative clauses: 'the medicine which helped me feel better.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I usually go jogging in the morning.
I go usually jogging in the morning.
Usually I go jogging in the morning always.
I go jogging usually in the morning.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of frequency usually go before the main verb: 'I usually go jogging.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: Could you tell me what time the pharmacy opens?
Could you tell me what time does the pharmacy open?
Could you tell me what time the pharmacy opens.
Could you tell me, what time the pharmacy opens?
questions.explanation: Indirect questions keep normal word order and end with a question mark: 'what time the pharmacy opens?'

questions.question: I ___ for two hours, so I need a break.
options: study
have studied
have been studying
studied
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an ongoing action: 'have been studying'.

questions.question: This umbrella isn't mine, it's ___.
options: her
hers
she
hers's
questions.explanation: Possessive pronoun (stands alone, no noun after it): 'it's hers.'

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses sequencing words.
options: First, warm up. After that, stretch your legs. Finally, start running.
First warm up after that stretch legs finally start running.
Finally warm up, first stretch, after that start running.
Warm up first, finally stretch, after that run.
questions.explanation: Sequencing words 'First,', 'After that,' and 'Finally,' correctly organize steps with commas.

questions.question: Every student ___ to bring a raincoat tomorrow.
options: need
needs
needing
are needing
questions.explanation: 'Every' takes a singular verb, even before a plural-sounding subject: 'Every student needs...'

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: It's freezing outside, isn't it?
It's freezing outside, is it?
It's freezing outside, doesn't it?
It's freezing outside, isn't?
questions.explanation: Positive statement + negative tag: 'It's freezing outside, isn't it?'
